title: A Judge-Aware Ranking Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models without Ground Truth
claim: Estimation error for latent quality and judge reliability decays steadily with more comparisons across problem sizes, confirming consistent estimation.
layout: 2x2 grid of log-log line plots, shared legend, reading left-to-right then down
description: A 2x2 grid of log-log line plots. Each panel shows a configuration (N,K) = (10,5), (20,10), (50,20), (100,20) in its title. The x-axis is the number of comparisons T, and the y-axis is mean squared error. Two curves appear in each panel. A blue line with circle markers shows MSE for the model scores s. An orange line with triangle markers shows MSE for the log judge-discrimination parameters γ. Shaded bands in matching colors show interquartile ranges. In every panel both curves fall steeply at small T, from about 10^2 down to 10^-1 or lower. They then decline roughly linearly on the log-log scale toward about 10^-2 to 10^-3 at the largest T. The curves nearly overlap in most panels. The legend sits in the top-right panel. The eye goes first to the steep initial drop at the top-left of each panel.
caption: MSE versus the number of comparisons $T$ for four configurations $(N,K)\in\{(10,5),(20,10),(50,20),(100,20)\}$. Both axes are logarithmic. Solid lines show means over $R=100$ runs, and shaded bands indicate interquartile ranges.
abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) on open-ended tasks without ground-truth labels is increasingly done via the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm. A critical but under-modeled issue is that judge LLMs differ substantially in reliability; treating all judges equally can yield biased leaderboards and misleading uncertainty estimates. More data can make evaluation more confidently wrong under misspecified aggregation. We propose a judge-aware ranking framework that extends the Bradley-Terry-Luce model by introducing judge-specific discrimination parameters, jointly estimating latent model quality and judge reliability from pairwise comparisons without reference labels. We establish identifiability up to natural normalizations and prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, enabling confidence intervals for score differences and rank comparisons. Across multiple public benchmarks and a newly collected dataset, our method improves agreement with human preferences, achieves higher data efficiency than unweighted baselines, and produces calibrated uncertainty quantification for LLM rankings.
